title: Stack, queue and linked-list concepts
learningObjectives: Explain the concept and its constraints.
Trace the example and reason about its data flow.
Identify complexity, boundary or safety considerations.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: A stack follows last-in, first-out order; a queue follows first-in, first-out order; a linked list stores nodes connected by pointers. Each structure supports different operation patterns and has different memory and complexity trade-offs.
understand.whyItMatters: Choosing a structure based on required operations helps avoid inefficient or unnecessarily complex implementations.
understand.analogy: Treat an algorithm or data structure as a set of operations that must preserve a clearly stated contract.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace formal complexity analysis, C object rules or algorithm preconditions.

explain.narrative:
A stack follows last-in, first-out order; a queue follows first-in, first-out order; a linked list stores nodes connected by pointers. Each structure supports different operation patterns and has different memory and complexity trade-offs.

Before implementation, state input constraints, empty-case behaviour, ownership and invariants. Compile with warnings and test representative, boundary and failure cases.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The stack stores two values and removes the most recently added value, 20. The example uses a fixed array and an index as the stack top.

practise.guidedTask: Draw the stack after each push and pop.
practise.independentTask: Implement a bounded queue with front, rear and count fields. Define full and empty conditions.
hints: A stack's pop operation must check that the stack is not empty.
A queue implementation must handle wrap-around when using a circular array.
A linked list requires careful allocation and release of every node.
